name: Paradise
tagline: 1990s UW–Madison parallel object-relational DBMS for GIS, built on SHORE for massive geographic datasets.
description: Paradise was a research database system from the University of Wisconsin–Madison database group that set out to store, browse and query very large geographic datasets by combining object-relational extensibility with shared-nothing parallelism. It provided an extended-relational data model with built-in raster, polygon, polyline, point and other spatial types, a subset of SQL for ad-hoc queries, a graphical front end for browsing results, and parallel query processing on top of the SHORE storage manager and the OPT++ extensible optimizer. The team evaluated it with the Sequoia 2000 GIS benchmark in a VLDB 1994 paper and described the parallel version at SIGMOD 1997. It never became a product, but its papers remain a key reference for declustering spatial data and running parallel spatial joins.
statusNote: UW–Madison research prototype (mid-1990s); never productized. Spatial ideas live on in PostGIS and parallel spatial engines.

pricing.notes: Only papers and the modified SHORE storage manager were published.

scale.notes: Designed to partition massive raster and vector datasets across a shared-nothing cluster.

strengths: Early end-to-end design for parallel processing of raster and vector GIS data
Built on the well-documented SHORE storage manager and OPT++ optimizer
Benchmarked publicly with Sequoia 2000, making results comparable
useCases: Research and teaching on parallel spatial databases
Background for spatial join and declustering techniques
